title: Request shaping and timeline-aware prefill prioritization to reduce attention-kernel latency tails
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Goal: reduce 95th/99th percentile latency spikes driven by attention-kernel hot switches during mixed v2/v3 workloads by shaping incoming requests and prioritizing prefill timelines. This ticket explores a timeline-aware admission controller that smooths bursts, staggers prefill work by priority, and couples soft-hysteresis to kernel-selection so we avoid thrashing between FlashAttention v2 and v3 implementations under bursty traffic.
acceptance_criteria: 95th percentile end-to-end prefill latency reduced by >= 20% on mixed v2/v3 model variants for our benchmark suite
Kernel selection oscillation metric (kernel_switches_per_minute) reduced by >= 60% under synthetic burst test
No regression in median latency or throughput for steady-state traffic profiles
Implemented feature gated behind 'timeline_shaping' flag with rollout plan and automated canary checks
Unit and integration tests added for admission controller behavior and prioritization ordering
updates: 2026-02-25: Created ticket after incident post-release where a burst of concurrent long-context prefill requests caused kernel oscillation and tail latency spikes. Initial triage indicates high-frequency kernel handoffs triggered by concurrency and shape of req arrival times.

2026-02-28: Spike analysis complete. Telemetry shows correlation between sudden influx of large-prefill jobs and two behaviors: (1) runtime prober flips to v3 for certain matrix shapes then flips back as decode latency dominates, (2) KV cache pressure forces workspace evictions causing extra allocations. Hypothesis: smoothing admission order will reduce oscillation.

2026-03-03: Prototype of a lightweight admission controller implemented (PR: github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/7893). Behavior: queue incoming requests for up to 15ms to batch small arrivals while applying a per-model timeline priority that favors ongoing decodes to complete prefill in order.

2026-03-06: Benchmarked prototype against synthetic burst harness (1000 concurrent prefill requests, varied seq_len). Results: median unchanged, 95th reduced ~18% but 99th still noisy. Observed residual oscillation due to immediate kernel prober reacting to first N samples — need soft hysteresis window.

2026-03-09: Added soft-hysteresis (hold selection for 250ms after change unless regression detected). Re-run benchmarks: 95th improved 24%, kernel_switches_per_minute down 72%. Side-effect: slight throughput dip (~2%) in extreme steady workloads.

2026-03-11: Design review with runtime and infra. Trade-offs discussed: hysteresis helps tail but may keep suboptimal kernel longer for specific sequences; fixed hold duration vs. adaptive hold based on workload variance debated. Agreement: rollout adaptive hold tuned by telemetry signals (variance of recent latency) with conservative defaults.

2026-03-12: Preparing canary config, feature flag 'timeline_shaping=v1' targeting 5% of traffic on dedicated cluster. Draft PR open for RFC and rollout runbook at docs.confluence.redwood/request-shaping-playbook.
Next: finalize adaptive hold algorithm, expand integration tests, and schedule Canary for 2026-03-15. Post-canary we'll run a day-long soak and look at regression windows before broader rollout.
risk_mitigation: Feature flag controlled rollout with kill-switch
Conservative default hysteresis and ability to switch to fixed small hold if regressions detected
Canary at 5% with automated alerts for tail regressions and kernel switch metrics
Rollback playbook documented in runbook link
notes_for_eng_review: Need feedback from kernel team on additional signals we can use to detect harmful oscillation (e.g., workspace allocation deltas, prober confidence scores)
Request infra to expose short-lived metric kernel_switches_per_minute as a high-cardinality metric for canary detection
Validation: add deterministic unit test for admission ordering when mixed payload sizes arrive concurrently
